blocks.text: So they come together facing each other, across so great a gulf Separated, as far as a ship could cross in three days. — — —

And Ammianus, book 22: Not far from there rises Carambis etc. Opposite which lies Criu-metopon, a promontory of the Taurica, separated from it by two thousand five hundred stadia. Strabo too, in book 2: Τὸ μὲν οὖν τῆς Εὐρώπης ἀκρωτήριον καλεῖται Κριοῦ μέτωπον, τὸ δὲ τῆς Ἀσίας Κάραμβις, διέχοντα ἀλλήλων περὶ δισχιλίους σαδίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους [To men oun tēs Eurōpēs akrōtērion kaleitai Kriou metōpon, to de tēs Asias Karambis, diechonta allēlōn peri dischilious sadious, kai pentakosious]· The promontory of Europe is called Criu-metopon (ram's forehead), and that of Asia Carambis, distant from each other about 2,500 stadia. These statements, however, are utterly false, and are openly refuted by Strabo's own words in book 3: Διέσηκε δὲ ἡ Κάραμβις τῆς μὲν τῶν Χερσονησιτῶν πόλεως σταδίους δισχιλίους, καὶ πεντακοσίους, τοῦ δὲ Κριοῦ μετώπου πολὺ ἐλάττους τὸν ἀριθμόν [Diesēke de hē Karambis tēs men tōn Chersonēsitōn poleōs stadious dischilious, kai pentakosious, tou de Kriou metōpou poly elattous ton arithmon]· Carambis is distant from the city of the Chersonesites by two thousand five hundred stadia, but from Criu-metopon by far less. Quite rightly: for Chersonesus the city is one thing, and Chersonesus the region, in which that city lies, another. The city, which is in the northern part of the Chersonese, is indeed 2,500 stadia distant from Carambis. But on the opposite side of the Chersonese, Criu-metopon is much nearer to Carambis. Yet these have been confused: what some had written about the city of Chersonesus, that it is 2,500 stadia from Carambis, was taken as if said of the whole Chersonese, and of its most southern part, namely Criu-metopon. The emptiness of this invention is especially apparent from what Strabo adds in the same place: Συχνοὶ γοῦν τῶν διαπλευσάντων τὸν πορθμὸν, ἅμα φασὶν ἀμφοτέρας ἰδεῖν τὰς ἄκρας ἑκατέρωθεν [Sychnoi goun tōn diapleusantōn ton porthmon, hama phasin amphoteras idein tas akras hekaterōthen]· Many of those who have sailed through this strait say that they saw both promontories at once, that is, when placed in the middle of the passage; which would not [col. 72] happen if the strait were 2,500 stadia wide. For the sight of the human eye is too weak to reach 1,250 stadia, which make more than 52 hourly leagues.

However that may be, the ancients relate that both in crossing this strait and on the rest of their journey the remarkable ingenuity of cranes shines forth. Pliny asserts that when about to fly across the Pontus they are steadied with ballast, and that when they have passed the middle, the pebbles are dropped from their feet, and when they have reached the mainland, the sand from their throat. That is, only then do they disgorge not pebbles but sand too. Solinus puts this more explicitly: Lest the force of the winds should resist them as they proceed to their destination, they swallow sand, and taking up little pebbles they [II, 620] ballast themselves to a moderate weight. And shortly after: When they know that they have come to the middle (of the Pontus), they free their feet of the load of stones. So sailors have reported, who have often been rained on by a shower of stones from this cause. The sand they do not disgorge until they are secure of their abode. Cassiodorus also mentions these pebbles, in Variae book 4, Letter 47: Cranes, when about to cross the sea, clasp small pebbles in their hooked feet, so that their lightness may not be carried off by too strong a wind, nor their native speed be weighed down by unequal burdens. The scholiast on Aristophanes' Birds, and Suidas following him, think that these pebbles are carried and thrown down by cranes for an entirely different reason: namely, so that from the sound of the falling stone they may perceive πότερον ἐπὶ γῆς, ἢ ἐπὶ θαλάσσης φέρωνται· καὶ εἰ μὲν ἐπὶ θαλάσσης ἥκοι ὁ λίθος ἀνύουσι τὴν ὁδόν· εἰ δὲ ἐπὶ γῆς, ἀναπαύονται [poteron epi gēs, ē epi thalassēs pherōntai; kai ei men epi thalassēs hēkoi ho lithos anyousi tēn hodon; ei de epi gēs, anapauontai], whether they are borne over land or over sea; if the stone falls into the sea, they continue on; but if onto land, they rest. But Maximus of Tyre, Oration 40, asserts that cranes carry this stone in their mouth as ballast. Οὐ πρότερον, he says, ἀνίπταται, πρὶν ξυλλάβῃ λίθον τῷ στόματι, ἕρμα μὲν εἶναι αὐτῇ πρὸς τὴν πτῆσιν, φυλακὴν δὲ πρὸς σωτηρίαν [Ou proteron … anuptatai, prin xyllabē lithon tō stomati, herma men einai autē pros tēn ptēsin, phylakēn de pros sōtērian]· It does not fly before it has taken up a stone in its beak, to be a support for its flight and a safeguard for its safety. Nor otherwise Nonnus, Dionysiaca book 40, line 521:

Αἱ στομάτων ἔκτοσθεν ἀοσσητῆρα κελεύθου Λᾶαν ἐλαφρίζουσι καταχθέα, μήποτε κείνων Ἱπταμένων πτερὰ κοῦφα παρακλάγξειεν ἀήτης. [Hai stomatōn ektosthen aossētēra keleuthou / Laan elaphrizousi katachthea, mēpote keinōn / Hiptamenōn ptera koupha paraklangxeien aētēs.]
Which carry in their mouth a heavy stone as a helper on their way, lest the wind should ever make the light wings of them as they fly go astray. And Philes, chapter 10:

Τίς ἕρμα ποιεῖ τῇσι γεράνοις τὰς λίθους, Ἃς ἐγκαθειργνύουσι τοῖς παρισθμίοις, Πρὸς τὰς ὑπὲρ γῆς ἐμβολὰς τῶν πνευμάτων; [Tis herma poiei tēsi geranois tas lithous, / Has enkatheirgnyousi tois paristhmiois, / Pros tas hyper gēs embolas tōn pneumatōn?]
